records.name: Aruba
records.summary:
An autonomous constituent country within a Western European kingdom, Aruba legislates positively rather than merely tolerating: its parliament voted 11-5 in 2016 to open registered unions carrying married-couple benefits (pension succession, emergency medical decisions) — the first island in the Caribbean to act, by its own government's account — and the official tourism authority runs a dedicated LGBT programme marketing the island as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly a hundred nationalities resident.

Travel-culture reporting through the kingdom's networks characterises Aruba, with its two sister islands, as quiet, tolerant and mostly open — a small, stable, tourism-dependent society. The parliamentary vote's own record notes religious and cultural opposition to full equal marriage, which remains unlegislated, and no local gender-recognition or specialist-care pathway is evidenced. No enforcement against trans or same-sex visitors is documented anywhere in the record: protection by registered partnership and tourism economics rather than full equality.

sources.claim: Aruba's official tourism website LGBT vacations page: markets Aruba ('One Happy Island') as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly 100 nationalities living together; general tourism promotion with an LGBT-specific landing page.
Aruba's official tourism site news item: Aruba voted for LGBT civil unions as the first island in the Caribbean - official promotion of the island's LGBT-inclusive development.

GlobalGayz travel-culture report (2017): 'Gay Life in a Tolerant Society in Aruba' - describes the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as quiet nests of gay-friendliness within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, with a tolerant and mostly open society; travel-oriented first-person perspective.

AP via Yahoo (Sept 2016): Aruba's parliament voted 11-5 (4 abstentions) to grant same-sex couples the right to register unions and receive benefits granted to married people (spousal pension, emergency medical decisions); previously couples married in the Netherlands could have certificates recognised; MP Desiree de Sousa Croes noted many islanders oppose same-sex unions on religious and cultural grounds.

records.name: Afghanistan
records.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. The 2024 Morality Law (PVPV) obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism"; the Taliban applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender Afghans report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that UN experts say is escalating into 2026.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.

sources.claim: European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA), Country Guidance on Afghanistan 2024, section 3.17 'LGBTIQ persons': assesses LGBTIQ persons as a profile at risk for international-protection purposes under Taliban rule.

EUAA Country of Origin Information report — Afghanistan Country Focus, section 4.5 'LGBTIQ+ persons': detailed COI on the situation of LGBTIQ+ persons, including punishment under the de facto authorities.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight report 'Even If You Go to the Skies, We'll Find You' (Jan 2022), based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans after the Taliban takeover. Documents Taliban members attacking or threatening people because of sexual orientation or gender identity, abuse from family members and neighbours who support the Taliban, people fleeing their homes, and lives built over years disappearing overnight.

Outright International report 'A Mountain on My Shoulders: 18 Months of Taliban Persecution of LGBTIQ Afghans' (Feb 2023), based on interviews with 22 LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country (Sept-Oct 2022). Finds Taliban security officials pursuing LGBTIQ people - especially gay men and trans women - more systematically than in the first months of rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention, and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations confirmed by the Taliban Supreme Court on social media.

DW report (Oct 2021) profiling 'Danish', a trans man hiding in a windowless back room in Kabul after the Taliban takeover, and his gay friend Khalid. Describes LGBTQ people facing the death penalty under Taliban rule and the only realistic option being to flee the country.

JURIST feature (Nov 2024) on findings by the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan, a group of Afghan LGBTQ+ refugees in Bremen. Documents systematic persecution under Taliban rule; notes that even before 2021 no legal framework protected LGBTQ people, and that transgender individuals are especially exposed.

Translation of Article 22 of the Taliban's PVPV (Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice) Law (July 2024) by the Afghanistan Justice Project. The article tasks morality enforcers with preventing a wide range of 'evils' including adultery and related conduct, codifying moral surveillance that reaches LGBTQ+ identity, women's public speech, and cultural expression.

OHCHR press release (Mar 2026): UN human-rights experts condemn the Taliban's surging use of public corporal punishment — at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double 2024 — warning women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for 'moral crimes' such as adultery, 'illicit relationships' and 'sodomy'.

Human Dignity Trust country profile: Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with severe penalties. (Only the opening of the profile was retrievable at fetch time.)
CNN (Nov 2024): 'LGBTQ Afghans say they face abuse in detention as Taliban crackdown intensifies' — first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody.

records.name: Angola
records.summary: Angola demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

sources.claim: Shadow report to the African Commission (81st session, Oct-Nov 2024) by Angolan LGBTIQ organisations (AIA, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, Movimento T, Queer People Alliance of Sex Workers, others) with Synergia and ILGA Pan-Africa. Documents discrimination and stigma, violence, barriers to healthcare including gender-affirming care, and obstacles to access to justice for LGBTQI+ people in Angola, with recommendations to the government.

Submission by Angolan organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, others) to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (74th pre-session). Addresses discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, barriers LGBT people face in accessing sexual and reproductive health, comprehensive sexuality education, gender-affirming care and education, and the lack of government-generated data on LGBT people in Angola.

SALC chapter 'Transgender Rights in Angola' (Laws and Policies Affecting Transgender Persons in Southern Africa): constitutional rights mapping (Article 23 does not list gender/SO as prohibited discrimination grounds, but 'other status' should be read to include them per UN Human Rights Committee); no specific law for gender-marker change, though section 87 of the 2015 Civil Registration Code gives the registrar general authority to alter records; employment discrimination prohibited under the 2015 Labour Law.

VICE (Oct 2019): overview of changing LGBTQ+ rights across Africa - 34 of 54 countries criminalise homosexuality; discusses the 'white person's problem' framing used to dismiss queer rights in Nigeria and the thorny, contested nature of legal change (context including Angola and Botswana).

BBC (April 2012): trans kuduro artist Titica takes Angola by storm - a trans woman singer/dancer who is the face of Angola's popular rap-techno fusion, named best kuduro artist 2011, performing at the presidential Divas concert - notable visibility for a trans person in a country where homosexuality was then illegal.

PinkNews (Feb 2021): Angola decriminalised homosexuality - the new penal code (adopted January 2019, effective February 2021) removed the Portuguese-colonial 'vice against nature' ban and introduced anti-discrimination protection, with discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation punishable by prison.

records.name: Anguilla
records.summary:
Anguilla's prohibitions were removed around 2000-2001 — a recent first-person travel account puts the change at 2000, the contemporaneous wire coverage of the Caribbean-wide reform at January 2001 — again by imposition from London after local reluctance; the earlier profile's 'decriminalised 2019' appeared in no source and has been deleted. Same-sex relationships are simply not an issue in the public sense because there is almost no public LGBT life: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers and same-sex wedding tourism pitched on 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere.'

A queer family travelling openly in 2023 described the experience as uneventful on a 35-square-mile island. The practical visitor picture is quiet neutrality — nothing protects you much, and little opposes you at all.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz report (2012): 'Gay Life in Anguilla' - a quiet 35-square-mile island where homosexuality is virtually a non-issue: no visible community, organisations, Pride events or gay venues; gay life minimal and private; scattered gay-friendly hotel lounges exist.
Gay Destination Weddings travel page for Anguilla: markets the British island as a wedding/honeymoon destination with top beaches and a 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere' for same-sex couples.

AP via SodomyLaws (Jan 2001): Britain scrapped homosexuality laws in its five Caribbean territories (Anguilla, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Montserrat, Turks and Caicos) by Order in Council after local legislatures refused - decriminalising consensual same-sex acts in private; local religious leaders objected, calling it a cultural rift with Britain.

AFAR magazine (June 2023): first-person travel piece - a queer family visiting Anguilla openly ('out and proud on a tiny Caribbean island'); notes gay sex decriminalised since 2000 and explores whether LGBTQ travellers are welcome in practice.

records.name: Albania
records.summary:
Albania is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; a National LGBTI Action Plan (2021–2027) is in force (implementation is admittedly flawed); and the UN Independent Expert on SOGI conducted a full country visit in July 2024 — a sign of government openness unusual for the region. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, no bathroom laws, no documented police targeting; the realistic risk is social hostility outside Tirana and along more conservative rural areas. EU candidate status is driving slow alignment.

sources.claim: End-of-mission statement of the UN Independent Expert on SOGI after his 1-12 July 2024 visit to Albania (Tirana plus five municipalities). Assesses implementation of national and international standards on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; notes cooperation from the government and identifies challenges and good practices.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Albania. Documents hate violence against trans people and sex workers (ten cases reported), LGBTI people's limited access to state services due to discrimination (civil society filling gaps with food packages, bill payments, reimbursement of documentation costs for IDs and passports), education barriers (30% of LGBTI respondents unable to complete compulsory education), and successful discrimination complaints.

Full report (A/HRC/59/43/Add.1, June 2025) of the UN Independent Expert on SOGI following the Albania visit. Evaluates Albania's adherence to human rights standards for LGBT people, examines the situation of lesbian, gay, bisexual and gender-diverse persons in depth, and makes recommendations on violence and discrimination.

PinkNews (Feb 2010): Albania passed an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation (but not same-sex marriage); homosexuality carried a 10-year sentence until 1995; welcomed by Albanian gay-rights groups and ILGA-Europe as a regional example.

Koha Jonë (Albanian, 2021): Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi called LGBT awareness meetings in Tirana high schools 'groups with a dubious agenda' and 'revolting' - example of anti-LGBT political rhetoric in Albania.

Koha Jonë (Albanian, 2021): politician Nard Ndoka called LGBT school meetings a 'terrible scandal' and claimed an 'LGBT government' was favouring the community in housing, education and employment - example of hostile political discourse.

Balkan Insight (Oct 2011): Albania's Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling-party MP Tritan Shehu for saying in parliament that 'homosexuality is disease and should be treated with hormones' - the commissioner urged parliament to guarantee LGBT community participation; homosexuality decriminalised in 1995.

records.name: Andorra
records.summary:
Andorra is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. The 2022 Law of the Person and Family modernised the legal framework (unified civil marriage, and legal gender recognition provisions); the Ministry of Equality now obliges all companies to maintain sexual and gender-based harassment protocols. ILGA-Europe records only three bias-motivated incidents in the most recent annual review — a tiny absolute number reflecting a small, safe, tourism-dependent country.

No traveler-facing concerns: no bathroom laws, no border issues (open border with Spain/France, though outside Schengen there are no document-gender checks), high social tolerance in practice despite a conservative Catholic history. Gaps: anti-discrimination coverage of gender identity is recent and shallower than Spain's; hate-crime law is generic rather than SOGI-specific. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Andorra. The 2022 Law of the Person and Family entered into force in February 2023, introducing legal gender recognition. A newspaper opinion piece linking trans identities to mental illness was removed after protest, with a public apology. DiversAnd met the Health Ministry on gender-affirming care protocols following the 2022 regulatory changes; microaggressions were reported but rarely to authorities, attributed to fear.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Andorra. Police record an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents per month; DiversAnd calls for a formal hate-crime registration system. In October a decree on trans-specific healthcare entered into force: HRT via the social security system from age 16, surgery from 18, and consultation coverage for under-16s. New workplace harassment protocols were criticised for not explicitly addressing gender diversity or trans-specific harassment.

Asher Fergusson LGBTQ+ Travel Safety Index (2023): ranks 203 countries for LGBTQ+ travel safety based on laws and international sources; also publishes a Global Transgender Rights Index - comparative travel-safety framework covering Andorra among all countries.

PinkNews (Sept 2023): Andorra's prime minister Xavier Espot Zamora came out as gay ('I never hid it'), saying he hoped it shows young people that anyone can 'reach the highest magistracy'; during his premiership Andorra legalised same-sex marriage, introduced gender identity/expression anti-discrimination laws, and trans rights.

GayLawNet Andorra laws page: age of consent 16 (Penal Code Article 206); registered-partner law since March 2005 gave same-sex partners some marriage rights; discrimination prohibited since 2005 - dated but specific legal reference.

records.name: United Arab Emirates
records.summary:
The UAE is one of the most thoroughly documented trans-traveler-hostile countries in the world. At the border, trans visitors have been X-rayed to check their genitals (Israeli trans women, detained and denied entry at Dubai airport), deported for having a male passport (Thai model Rachaya Noppakaroon at Expo 2020; Gigi Gorgeous), denied entry despite valid UAE visas (Indian trans person), and sentenced to prison for "dressing in a feminine way" (Singaporean trans woman, 1 year in Abu Dhabi). A Brazilian trans woman was arrested in her Dubai apartment by plainclothes police accusing her of drug trafficking.

The state "employs various legal mechanisms to explicitly acknowledge and penalize nonconformity with traditional gender roles" and actively targets "non-Emirati tourists." There is no legal gender recognition.

However, the UAE does not have the death penalty for same-sex conduct (unlike Saudi Arabia or Iran), no documented custodial death of a trans person (unlike Saudi), and some trans visitors do enter successfully if their passport gender matches their presentation. The targeting is triggered by passport/presentation mismatch, not blanket.

sources.claim: Ynetnews report on two Israeli trans women denied entry to Dubai (2025): detained for hours at the airport, subjected to repeated physical examinations including X-ray checks 'to see whether we had male or female genitals' despite passports listing them as female, mocked by staff, and deported. Illustrates anatomy-based screening of trans travellers at UAE borders.

Vice report (March 2022): Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, travelling with a team of 14 to perform at Expo 2020 Dubai, was stopped at immigration, interrogated for nine hours, and deported despite valid documents - reportedly because her passport still showed her male gender marker.

Brazilian outlet Metropoles (April 2023, in Portuguese): a Brazilian trans woman was arrested in Dubai in September 2022 after police (investigating her acquaintance for drug trafficking) accused her of drug offences when she failed a toxicological exam; she accuses the Brazilian embassy of negligence. Shows trans visitors can be swept into the UAE criminal system with thin consular support.

Cairo 52 legal review of the UAE: multiple legal mechanisms explicitly penalise non-conformity with traditional gender roles; trans expression (appearance or accessories) frequently leads to arrest, detention or deportation of non-Emirati tourists and residents. Legal gender recognition is severely constrained; a recent medical liability law explicitly prohibits gender-affirming healthcare for non-intersex people. Article 359 and related provisions criminalise cross-dressing and 'imitation of women'.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the 2022 federal criminal code criminalises consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment (complaint-based enforcement). Article 412 penalises 'any man who disguises himself as a woman to enter a woman-only space' - a provision used to prosecute trans women and gender-nonconforming people. No legal gender recognition; no LGBTI organisations able to register.

TMZ report (Aug 2016): Canadian trans model Gigi Gorgeous was detained at Dubai airport and denied entry; she says the immigration officer told her 'I was told you are transgender. You cannot come into the country.' Dubai authorities cited the passport; 'imitation of women by men' is illegal in Dubai.

records.name: Argentina
records.summary:
Argentina has one of the world's most progressive legal frameworks — the 2012 Gender Identity Law allows administrative self-identification (no medical requirements), offers an X marker for non-binary people, and funds transition healthcare. Buenos Aires is "one of the safest major cities in Latin America for LGBTQ+ visitors."

But the situation is deteriorating sharply under the Milei government: the president has called "gender ideology" "child abuse," issued decrees modifying the Gender Identity Law, and hate crimes hit a record 227 in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours — trans women bearing the brunt). Police institutional violence against trans and travesti women is documented (arbitrary raids, drug-law criminalisation, searches only on travestis). The violence targets local vulnerable communities rather than tourists, but the trajectory is concerning.

The 2012 self-ID law remains in force for adults and courts are pushing back on the Milei decrees.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (Apr 2025): 'Argentina's transgender community confronts a 'chaotic, desperate' situation' under the Milei government — rollback of trans health and recognition policies amid rising hostility.

Agencia Presentes (Mar 2026, Spanish): 'Hate crimes in Argentina: increase and a record of one every 38 hours' — the National Observatory of LGBT+ Hate Crimes recorded 227 hate crimes in 2025, a record — on average one every 38 hours.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 500); the underlying Agencia Presentes article (Feb 2025) reports that President Milei modified the Gender Identity Law by decree and explains why organisations asked the courts to intervene.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2025) covers Argentina's decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Argentina was long a regional leader - first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality (2010) and one of the world's most progressive gender identity laws (2012, legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval), with nonbinary markers recognised and trans employment quotas. Since Milei took office in December 2023, documented rollbacks include elimination of the Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity and closure of the anti-discrimination institute.

misterb&b gay travel guide to Buenos Aires safety (2026): describes Buenos Aires as one of the safest major cities in Latin America for LGBTQ+ visitors, citing the 2010 marriage law and 2012 self-ID gender law; same-sex couples holding hands in Palermo, Recoleta and San Telmo draw no particular reaction. Travel-oriented, gay-male-focused perspective.

Wikipedia article on Argentina's Gender Identity Law (Law 26,743, effective June 2012): allows transgender people to be treated according to their self-perceived gender identity in government documents and healthcare, without requiring surgery, diagnosis or judicial approval - the first law of its kind globally.

Infobae (April 2025, in Spanish): Argentina's Supreme Court upheld the life sentence of the murderer of trans activist Diana Sacayán (killed 2015), declining to reinstate the 'travesticidio' hate-based aggravating factor that lower courts had removed - a signal about how hate-motive recognition for anti-trans killings is contested in the courts.
